blocks.text: The Chaldee translators too, and the Syriac and the Samaritan, differ little from these. Jonathan has צירא tsajera; Onkelos קריא kadja; Joseph the Blind קיפופא kiphupha; the Syriac ܥܘܕܐ auda; and the Samaritan ࠑࠃࠉࠀ tsadja. These words, however different in appearance, nevertheless come to almost the same thing. Thus the Samaritan ࠑࠃࠉࠀ tsadja is the female of the little owl, which, as the Arabs taught us above, is called in Arabic صدى [ṣadā] tsada, with the same radicals. And Jonathan's צירא is a corrupt word: in its place one should write צדיא, as the same author has at Deut. XIV, 16. Nor is Onkelos's קריא anything else, nor the Syriac ܥܘܕܐ ^{(1)}. For that the letters Tsade, Koph and Ajin are interchangeable is shown by the Chaldee ארעא and ארקא for ארץ, earth. And as for קיפופא kiphupha in Joseph the Blind: if it is not the same as צדיא tsadja or קריא kadjah, that it is at least a kindred animal is proved from a passage of the Talmud in Nidda, ch. 3, fol. 23a, in which קריא וקפופא, kadja and kiphupha (so it should be read, not [III, 16] קריא karja, as our editions wrongly have it ^{(2)}), are counted among the animals דעיניהן הולכות לפניהן כשל אדם, whose eyes look forward like a human's, whereas in the other birds the eyes are at the side. Hence the Gloss there: קריא וקפופא עוף הצועק בלילה ופניו דומות לחתול ועיניו לפניו, Kadja (so I read for קריא karja) and Kiphupha, a bird which cries at night, and has a face like a cat's, and eyes in front ^{(3)}. This is a description of the little owl or the eagle owl. Therefore, if you except Symmachus, for whom כוס chos is the hoopoe, all the ancients understand by this name the little owl, the night raven or the eagle owl, birds that do not differ much from one another. And if in these words of Jerome, but Symmachus the hoopoe, you read ululam [owl] for upupam [hoopoe], there will be no notable disagreement among the ancients, since the night birds, the little owl, eagle owl, owl and night raven, are so similar to one another that writers commonly use the names interchangeably.

To these are added the more recent Hebrews, who hold that it is called כוס chos as if כוסה chose, that is, hiding itself or lying hidden, because this bird נכסה מן העין, shuns sight, or נכסה מעין אדם, hides itself from the eyes of men. So Baal Hatturim and Aben Ezra. And R. Selomo on Leviticus: כוס וינשוף הם צוא״טיש הצועקי׳ בלילה ויש להם לסתות כאדם, Chos and jansuph, in French chovettes, birds which hoot at night and have jaws like a man. This is partly taken from the passage of the Talmud cited above, where precisely this is asserted of the birds קריא and קפופא. Since these words of R. Selomo are explicit, I cannot at all understand what these words of Kimchi in his Lexicon refer to: כוס שם עוף טמא לא נודע אצלנו ורבינו שלמה ז״ל פי׳ פלקו״ן בלע״ז ואותו שקורין פלקו״ן הוא נמצא ביישוב וצרין בו בני האדם שאר העופות ואחר שאמר הכתוב ככוס חרבות ידמה שהוא מדברי, Chos, the name of an unknown bird. Our master R. Selomo of blessed memory explains it in the vernacular as falcon. But the bird they call falcon is found in inhabited places, and men use it to hunt other birds; whereas Scripture, since it says “Like the chos of the wilderness”, seems to mean a bird living in the desert. In these words he ascribes to R. Selomo an opinion very different from the one his Commentaries present. Yet, following this, David de Pomis, Münster, Arias and others render כוס chos as falcon. Indeed, as if one were free to invent anything here, because Kimchi says it is an unknown [col. 275] bird, some render it cuckoo, others illex [decoy bird], others screech owl, others pelican, and what not? It must be admitted, meanwhile, that by far the greatest part [III, 17] of the modern translators too have kept the little owl. And Drusius endeavours to prove that this is the true sense of the word from the German kuts for little owl and the Paduan chus for scops, a kind of little owl, words which seem to come close to the Hebrew כוס chos, as if derived from it. So it will seem dangerous to oppose such great agreement ^{(4)}. I shall nevertheless say what I once conjectured about this word, not without some appearance of truth.

I suspected that the word כוס chos signifies the truo, or, what is the same, the onocrotalus. For the bird the Greeks call ὀνοκρόταλος [onokrotalos] the Romans called TRUO. Now trua is a kind of vessel.
When the woman saw the ladle so wonderfully topped with a crest.
When the great bronze pot boils, the cook stirs it a little with a ladle.
